title: Secure File Upload
summary: Hardens upload endpoints by checking type, size, name and storage location, blocking path traversal, executable content and image bombs.
description: An upload endpoint accepts bytes from strangers and writes them to your disk. Done carelessly, it becomes remote code execution, stored XSS, or an easy way to fill the volume. This skill reviews each step from the request to the stored file.

It replaces trust in the client with checks on the server: what the content really is, how big it can be, where it is stored and how it is served back. The result is a short, enforced policy rather than a list of hopes.
useWhen: You are adding avatars, attachments or document import
A file uploaded under a trusted name ended up served as HTML
Disk usage or memory spikes during uploads
A review found filenames used directly in paths
body:
# Secure file upload

Never trust the filename, the extension or the Content-Type header from the client.

## Steps

1. Find every upload handler (multipart parsers, presigned URL generators, import jobs) and follow a file from request to final location and later download.
2. Size: set a hard limit at the parser and at the proxy, and stream to storage instead of reading the whole file into memory. Limit the number of files per request.
3. Type: allow a short list of extensions, then verify the content with magic bytes (file signature) or a library, and make sure both agree. For images, re-encode with a trusted library; this strips embedded scripts and metadata, and caps pixel dimensions to stop decompression bombs.
4. Name: discard the original name. Generate a random one (UUID) and keep the original only as display metadata, escaped on output. Reject names with `..`, slashes, null bytes or reserved Windows names.
5. Location: store outside the web root, or in object storage with a private bucket. Resolve the final path and confirm it starts with the base directory. Never write with execute permission.
6. Serving: send `Content-Disposition: attachment` for non-images, set `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and use a separate domain for user files where possible. Check authorization on download.
7. Archives: when unzipping, check each entry path against the destination and cap total expanded size.
8. Consider malware scanning for files shared between users.

## Rules

- A blocklist of "bad extensions" is not a defence.
- Add tests: a `.php` file renamed `.jpg`, `../../x` as the name, an oversized file, an empty file.

## Report

Handlers reviewed, issues fixed with `path:line`, limits chosen, and tests added.

example.prompt: Make the avatar and invoice upload endpoints safe.
example.result: avatar.ts: now re-encodes to WebP, max 5 MB and 4000 px, stored as a random id in a private bucket. invoice.ts: PDFs only, verified by signature, 20 MB cap, streamed. Fixed a traversal in invoice.ts:58 where the original name was joined into the path. Downloads send attachment and nosniff. 9 tests added.

faq.question: Why re-encode images?
faq.answer: A re-encoded image contains only pixels your library produced, so hidden payloads and odd metadata are dropped along the way.

faq.question: Is checking the extension and MIME type enough?
faq.answer: No. Both come from the client. Reading the file signature and re-processing the content are what give real assurance.

access: Reads and edits upload handlers and storage code
Runs your tests with sample hostile files you can inspect first
